_note: ORIGINAL word-study items for Grades 4-6 (Al-Anjal platform): dictation, spelling rules, sound-spelling, syllables, affixes, roots, homophones. Written for this platform; no list or item is copied from a published program. Loaded by the question seed (withWordStudyItems) when this file exists.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Hop has one short vowel and ends in one consonant, so the p is doubled before -ing: hop → hopping.
explanation.tip: One syllable, one short vowel, one last consonant: double it before -ing.

dictation.sentence: The rabbit kept hopping across the yard.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Smile ends in a silent e. Drop the e before -ing: smile → smiling.
explanation.tip: Drop the silent e before an ending that starts with a vowel.

dictation.sentence: Everyone was smiling at the end of the race.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Cry ends in a consonant + y, so y changes to i before -ed: cry → cried.
explanation.tip: Consonant + y: change the y to i before -ed.

dictation.sentence: The baby cried until her bottle was ready.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Bright has the long i sound spelled igh (the g and h are silent), then -est.
explanation.tip: Long i before t is often spelled with three letters, two of them silent.

dictation.sentence: The brightest star rose over the desert.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Thirst is spelled with ir (r-controlled), then -y is added.
explanation.tip: Listen for the vowel + r sound and remember which spelling this word uses (er, ir or ur).

dictation.sentence: We were thirsty after the long walk.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Kneel starts with a silent k, and the long e is spelled ee.
explanation.tip: Some words that start with the /n/ sound have a silent letter before the n.

dictation.sentence: Please kneel down to tie your shoe.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Toast has long o spelled oa; add -er for the machine that toasts.
explanation.tip: Long o in the middle of a word is often spelled with a vowel team.

dictation.sentence: Dad fixed the old toaster on Saturday.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Shrimp begins with the digraph sh and the blend r: s-h-r, and ends with the blend mp.
explanation.tip: Say each sound slowly; write every consonant and no extra vowel.

dictation.sentence: We ate shrimp at the beach cafe.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Brave keeps its silent e before -ly, because -ly starts with a consonant.
explanation.tip: Keep the silent e before an ending that starts with a consonant.

dictation.sentence: She bravely spoke in front of the class.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: The /oi/ sound in the middle of a word is spelled oi; then add -ed.
explanation.tip: In the middle of a word this vowel sound is usually oi; at the end it is usually oy.

dictation.sentence: The milk spoiled in the hot car.

items.stem: Add -ing to swim. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: Swim: one syllable, one short vowel, one final consonant → double the m: swimming.
explanation.tip: Check the base word: one short vowel and one last consonant? Double it.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Swim has one short vowel and ends in one consonant, so the m must be doubled.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Only ONE extra m is added: double the last consonant once.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Swim has no silent e; do not add an e before -ing.

items.stem: Add -ed to bake. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: Bake ends in silent e, so just add -d: baked.
explanation.tip: A word that ends in silent e takes only -d.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Bake already ends in e. Drop that e (or just add -d); do not write two e's.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Bake has a long a with a silent e, so the k is not doubled.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The e must stay in the -ed ending: b-a-k-e-d.

items.stem: Add -ed to try. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: Try ends in consonant + y: change y to i and add -ed → tried.
explanation.tip: Consonant + y → change the y to i before -ed and -es.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Try ends in a consonant + y, so change the y to i before -ed.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is spelled the way it sounds; the base word try must still be seen: tr + ied.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Change the y to i — do not keep both the y and the i.

items.stem: Add -ed to play. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: Play ends in vowel + y, so the y stays: played.
explanation.tip: Vowel + y keeps the y; consonant + y changes to i.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Play ends in a VOWEL + y (ay), so the y stays: do not change y to i.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The ending is -ed: keep the e.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Plaid is a different word (a cloth pattern). After a vowel, the y does not change.

items.stem: Add -er to big. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: Big → double the g → bigger.
explanation.tip: Short vowel + one consonant at the end: double before -er and -est.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Big has one short vowel and one final consonant, so double the g before -er.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The ending -er has only one e.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The ending -er needs its vowel e.

items.stem: Add -est to cute. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: Cute: drop the silent e, add -est → cutest.
explanation.tip: Silent e is dropped before -er and -est.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Cute ends in silent e. Drop it before -est, which starts with a vowel.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Cute has a long u (silent e), so the t is not doubled.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The ending is spelled -est, not -ist.

items.stem: Write the plural of baby. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: Baby ends in consonant + y → babies.
explanation.tip: Consonant + y: change y to i, then add -es.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Baby ends in a consonant + y: change y to i and add -es.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Change the y to i before -es.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The plural ending is -es: b-a-b-i-e-s.

items.stem: Add -ful to hope. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: Hope + ful keeps the e → hopeful.
explanation.tip: Keep the silent e before a consonant ending (-ful, -ly, -ment).

options.label: A
options.rationale: Keep the silent e before -ful, because -ful starts with a consonant.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The suffix -ful has only one l.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Hope has a long o with a silent e; nothing is doubled.

items.stem: Which word has the long a sound spelled ay?

explanation.whyCorrect: Stray ends with the long a sound spelled ay.
explanation.tip: At the end of a word, long a is often spelled ay.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Train has long a, but it is spelled ai, not ay.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Snack has a short a sound.

options.label: D
options.rationale: In paw, aw spells a different vowel sound (as in saw).

items.stem: Which word has the same vowel sound as boil?

explanation.whyCorrect: Boil and toy share the /oi/ sound (spelled oi and oy).
explanation.tip: The /oi/ sound is spelled oi in the middle of a word and oy at the end.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Tool has the oo sound, not the oi sound.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Bowl has a long o sound.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Bell has a short e sound.

items.stem: Which word has the same vowel + r sound as bird?

explanation.whyCorrect: Bird and turn share the same vowel + r sound (ir and ur sound alike).
explanation.tip: er, ir and ur often sound the same; ar and or sound different.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Barn has the ar sound, as in car.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Born has the or sound, as in fork.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Bead has a long e sound and no r.

items.stem: What is the FIRST sound you hear in knot?

explanation.whyCorrect: In kn, the k is silent, so knot begins with /n/.
explanation.tip: kn at the start of a word: the k is silent.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The k in kn is silent: you do not hear it.

options.label: B
options.rationale: In kn only the n is heard; the k is a silent letter.

options.label: D
options.rationale: There is no w in knot.

items.stem: Which word has the long i sound spelled igh?

explanation.whyCorrect: Slight spells long i with igh (the g and h are silent).
explanation.tip: igh says long i; eigh usually says long a.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Slit has a short i sound.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Slide spells long i with i and a silent e, not igh.

options.label: D
options.rationale: In sleigh, eigh spells a long a sound.

items.stem: Which word begins with the same sound as phone?

explanation.whyCorrect: ph says /f/, so phone and fence begin with the same sound.
explanation.tip: p + h together say /f/ (phone, graph).

options.label: B
options.rationale: ph says /f/, not /p/.

options.label: C
options.rationale: v makes a buzzing sound; ph says /f/ with no buzz.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The h is part of ph; together they say /f/.

items.stem: Which shows the correct way to split rabbit into syllables?

explanation.whyCorrect: Two consonants between vowels (VC/CV): split between them → rab-bit.
explanation.tip: Double consonants in the middle: split between them.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Split between the two b's: each syllable gets one consonant.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Split between the double consonants, not after them.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Every syllable needs a vowel; r alone is not a syllable.

items.stem: Which shows the correct way to split tiger into syllables?

explanation.whyCorrect: Tiger has a long i, so the first syllable ends with the vowel (open syllable): ti-ger.
explanation.tip: Long vowel sound first? Try splitting after the vowel (V/CV).

options.label: A
options.rationale: Tig- would have a short i, but tiger has a long i: the first syllable is open (ti-).

options.label: B
options.rationale: Every syllable needs a vowel; t alone is not a syllable.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The last syllable needs its vowel: -ger.

items.stem: Which shows the correct way to split napkin into syllables?

explanation.whyCorrect: Two consonants between vowels: split between them → nap-kin.
explanation.tip: VC/CV: split between the two middle consonants.

options.label: A
options.rationale: pk is not a blend that starts a syllable; split between p and k.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Split between the two middle consonants, p and k.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Every syllable needs a vowel; n alone is not a syllable.

items.stem: How many syllables are in basketball?

explanation.whyCorrect: bas-ket-ball: three vowel sounds, three syllables.
explanation.tip: Count the vowel sounds (or clap the beats).

options.label: B
options.rationale: Clap it: bas-ket-ball has three beats.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Clap it: bas-ket-ball has three beats, not four.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Each vowel sound makes a syllable: there are three.

items.stem: Add a prefix to kind to make a word that means “not kind.”

explanation.whyCorrect: un- means “not”: unkind = not kind.
explanation.tip: un- = not; re- = again; pre- = before; mis- = wrongly.

options.label: A
options.rationale: re- means “again,” not “not.”

options.label: B
options.rationale: pre- means “before,” not “not.”

options.label: C
options.rationale: mis- means “wrongly,” not “not.”

items.stem: Which word means “to write again”?

explanation.whyCorrect: re- means “again”: rewrite = write again.
explanation.tip: re- = again.

options.label: A
options.rationale: un- means “not” or “undo,” not “again.”

options.label: B
options.rationale: mis- means “wrongly,” not “again.”

options.label: D
options.rationale: pre- means “before,” not “again.”

items.stem: Which word means “to heat before”?

explanation.whyCorrect: pre- means “before”: preheat = heat before (the oven, before baking).
explanation.tip: pre- = before.

options.label: A
options.rationale: re- means “again”: reheat = heat again.

options.label: C
options.rationale: un- means “not,” and unheat is not a word.

options.label: D
options.rationale: mis- means “wrongly.”

items.stem: Add mis- to spell. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: Add a prefix without changing the base word: mis + spell = misspell.
explanation.tip: Prefixes never change the spelling of the base word.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Keep every letter: mis + spell = misspell, with two s's.

options.label: C
options.rationale: un- means “not”; the word that means “spell wrongly” uses mis-.

options.label: D
options.rationale: re- means “again”; the word that means “spell wrongly” uses mis-.

items.stem: Which word means “full of joy”?

explanation.whyCorrect: -ful means “full of”: joyful = full of joy.
explanation.tip: -ful = full of; -less = without.

options.label: A
options.rationale: -less means “without”: joyless = without joy.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The suffix -ful has only one l.

options.label: C
options.rationale: -ness means “the state of being,” and joyness is not a word.

items.stem: Which word means “a person who teaches”?

explanation.whyCorrect: -er can mean “a person who”: teacher = a person who teaches.
explanation.tip: -er (and -or) can mean “a person who.”

options.label: A
options.rationale: -ful means “full of,” not “a person who.”

options.label: B
options.rationale: -less means “without.”

options.label: D
options.rationale: -ly means “in a way”; it does not name a person.

items.stem: Which word means “without fear”?

explanation.whyCorrect: -less means “without”: fearless = without fear.
explanation.tip: -less = without.

options.label: A
options.rationale: -ful means “full of”: fearful is the opposite.

options.label: C
options.rationale: -ness means “the state of being,” and fearness is not a word.

options.label: D
options.rationale: -ly means “in a way,” and fearly is not a word.

items.stem: What does the suffix add to each word?

explanation.whyCorrect: -less = without; -er = a person who; -ness = the state of being; -ly = in a way.
explanation.tip: Cover the base word and read the suffix alone.

items.stem: We could not ____ the music over the noise.

explanation.whyCorrect: Hear (with your ear) means to listen.
explanation.tip: Hear has the word ear inside it.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Here is a place word (come here). Hear means to listen with your ears.

options.label: B
options.rationale: A hare is an animal like a rabbit.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is not a word; hear has ear in it — you hear with your ear.

items.stem: The wind ____ the papers off the desk.

explanation.whyCorrect: Blew is the past tense of blow.
explanation.tip: Sound-alike words: check the meaning, then the spelling.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Blue is a colour. Blew is the past of blow.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The sentence is about the past, so it needs blew.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is not a word; the past of blow is spelled b-l-e-w.

items.stem: Which rule do you use to add -ing to each word?

explanation.whyCorrect: sitting (short vowel + one consonant), making and sliding (drop e), crying (y stays before -ing), jumping (two consonants: just add).
explanation.tip: Look at the end of the base word before adding the ending.

items.stem: Which rule do you use to add -ed to each word?

explanation.whyCorrect: hugged (double), copied (consonant + y → i), stayed (vowel + y stays), smiled (ends in e: add -d).
explanation.tip: Consonant + y changes; vowel + y stays.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Begin is stressed on the last syllable (be-GIN), so the n is doubled before -ing.
explanation.tip: Two syllables, stress on the last one, one short vowel + one consonant: double it.

dictation.sentence: The beginning of the film was exciting.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Happy ends in consonant + y: change y to i before -ness.
explanation.tip: Consonant + y: change y to i before most suffixes.

dictation.sentence: Their happiness filled the whole room.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Care keeps its silent e before -ful, and -ful has only one l.
explanation.tip: The suffix that means “full of” has only one l.

dictation.sentence: Be careful with the glass bowl.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Wrinkle starts with a silent w, and ends with -le.
explanation.tip: Some words that start with /r/ have a silent letter before the r.

dictation.sentence: There is a wrinkle in my shirt.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Thought is spelled ough (the g and h are silent), then -ful with one l.
explanation.tip: This word has a four-letter vowel spelling with two silent letters.

dictation.sentence: It was a thoughtful gift from my aunt.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Explore drops its silent e before -er: explore → explorer.
explanation.tip: Drop the silent e before an ending that starts with a vowel.

dictation.sentence: The explorer crossed the frozen river.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Value drops its e before -able: value → valuable.
explanation.tip: Drop the final e before -able.

dictation.sentence: The museum keeps valuable old coins.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Apply ends in consonant + y: change y to i before -ed, and keep the double p.
explanation.tip: Consonant + y: change y to i before -ed.

dictation.sentence: She applied glue to the paper.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Shoulder spells its long o sound with ou, then -der.
explanation.tip: The long o sound in this word is spelled with a vowel team that usually says /ow/.

dictation.sentence: He carried the bag on his shoulder.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Fountain: /ow/ spelled ou, then -tain.
explanation.tip: The /ow/ sound in the middle of a word is often spelled ou.

dictation.sentence: Children splashed in the fountain.

items.stem: Add -ed to plan. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: Plan: short vowel + one consonant → double the n → planned.
explanation.tip: Double the last consonant to keep the vowel short.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Planed would rhyme with “caned” (a long a). Plan has a short a, so double the n.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Keep the e of the -ed ending.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The -ed ending has one e.

items.stem: Add -ing to shine. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: Shine: drop the silent e, add -ing → shining.
explanation.tip: Silent e words: drop the e before -ing.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Drop the silent e before -ing.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Shinning would have a short i (like winning). Shine has a long i: do not double.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Spell the whole -ing ending.

items.stem: Add -s to carry. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: Carry → carries (consonant + y → ies).
explanation.tip: Consonant + y: change y to i, add -es.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Carry ends in consonant + y: change y to i and add -es.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Change the y to i before -es.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Keep the i: c-a-r-r-i-e-s.

items.stem: Add -ed to enjoy. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: Enjoy ends in vowel + y: just add -ed → enjoyed.
explanation.tip: Vowel + y: keep the y and add the ending.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Enjoy ends in vowel + y (oy), so the y stays.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Keep the e of the -ed ending.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Never double a y.

items.stem: Add -ing to begin. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: be-GIN: stressed last syllable, short vowel + one consonant → double → beginning.
explanation.tip: In two-syllable words, double only when the LAST syllable is stressed.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Begin is stressed on its last syllable (be-GIN), so double the n.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Double the n once only.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Add only -ing to the base word begin.

items.stem: Add -ful to use. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: Use + ful keeps the e → useful.
explanation.tip: Keep the e before a consonant ending.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Keep the silent e before -ful (a consonant ending).

options.label: C
options.rationale: The suffix -ful has one l.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Use already has its e; do not add another.

items.stem: Add -ness to lazy. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: Lazy → lazi + ness → laziness.
explanation.tip: Consonant + y: change y to i, even before -ness.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Lazy ends in consonant + y: change y to i before -ness.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The suffix -ness has two s's.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Lazy has a long a; the z is not doubled.

items.stem: Add -ed to visit. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: VIS-it: the last syllable is not stressed, so just add -ed → visited.
explanation.tip: Stress on the first syllable: do not double.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Visit is stressed on the FIRST syllable (VIS-it), so the t is not doubled.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Keep the i of the base word: vis-it.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The ending is spelled -ed.

items.stem: Which word has the same vowel sound as crowd?

explanation.whyCorrect: Crowd and mouth share the /ow/ sound (spelled ow and ou).
explanation.tip: ow can say /ow/ (cow) or long o (snow): read the word to check.

options.label: A
options.rationale: In snow, ow spells a long o sound.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Mud has a short u sound.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Moth has a short o sound.

items.stem: In which word does ea spell the short e sound?

explanation.whyCorrect: In bread, ea spells short e.
explanation.tip: ea has three sounds: long e (beach), short e (bread), long a (great).

options.label: B
options.rationale: In beach, ea says long e.

options.label: C
options.rationale: In great, ea says long a.

options.label: D
options.rationale: In bear, ea + r makes the /air/ sound.

items.stem: Which word has a silent letter?

explanation.whyCorrect: In thumb, the b after m is silent.
explanation.tip: mb at the end of a word: the b is silent.

options.label: A
options.rationale: In thump, both m and p are heard.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Every letter in plum is heard.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Every letter in tub is heard.

items.stem: Which word has the /f/ sound spelled gh?

explanation.whyCorrect: In laugh, gh spells /f/.
explanation.tip: gh can be silent (night), say /f/ (laugh) or say /g/ (ghost).

options.label: A
options.rationale: In caught, gh is silent.

options.label: B
options.rationale: At the start of a word, gh says /g/.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Half spells /f/ with the letter f.

items.stem: Which word has the same vowel sound as cause?

explanation.whyCorrect: Cause and straw share the vowel sound spelled au and aw.
explanation.tip: au usually comes before a consonant; aw comes at the end or before n, l.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Stray has a long a sound.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Stew has the /oo/ sound spelled ew.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Star has the ar sound.

items.stem: Which word ends with /shun/ spelled -tion?

explanation.whyCorrect: Motion ends with -tion, the most common spelling of /shun/.
explanation.tip: /shun/ at the end of a word is usually -tion.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Ocean spells its /sh/ sound with ce.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Mansion spells /shun/ with -sion.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Cushion spells its /sh/ sound with sh.

items.stem: Which shows the correct way to split rocket into syllables?

explanation.whyCorrect: Rocket has a short o, so the first syllable is closed: rock-et (ck stays together).
explanation.tip: Short vowel? Keep the consonant with the first syllable (VC/V).

options.label: A
options.rationale: Ro- would have a long o; rocket has a short o, so the c-k stays with the first syllable.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Every syllable needs a vowel; r alone is not a syllable.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Every syllable needs a vowel; t alone is not a syllable.

items.stem: Which shows the correct way to split pilot into syllables?

explanation.whyCorrect: Pilot has a long i: split after the vowel → pi-lot.
explanation.tip: Try V/CV first; if the word sounds wrong, try VC/V.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Pil- would have a short i; pilot has a long i, so the first syllable is open.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Every syllable needs a vowel.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Every syllable needs a vowel; t alone is not a syllable.

items.stem: Which shows the correct way to split hundred into syllables?

items.stem: How many syllables are in unbelievable?

items.stem: Which word means “to not agree”?

items.stem: Which word means “not regular”?

items.stem: Which word means “able to be washed”?

options.label: D

items.stem: Which word means “full of danger”?

options.label: C
options.rationale: -less means “without.”

options.label: D

items.stem: Which suffix meaning goes with each word?

explanation.whyCorrect: -able = can be; -ment = act or result of; -ous = full of.
explanation.tip: Find the suffix at the end, then say its meaning.

items.stem: She ____ the answer before the teacher asked.

options.label: C

items.stem: The baker needs more ____ for the bread.

options.label: A

options.label: D

items.stem: Which rule do you use to add -er or -est?

items.stem: Which rule do you use to add the suffix?

explanation.whyCorrect: happiness, hopeless, sadly (no doubling before a consonant ending), plentiful.
explanation.tip: Endings that start with a consonant: keep the e and do not double.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

items.stem: Listen to the word and the sentence. Type the word you hear.

items.stem: Add -ed to refer. Which spelling is correct?

explanation.whyCorrect: re-FER: stress on the last syllable → double the r → referred.
explanation.tip: Stressed last syllable + one vowel + one consonant: double.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Refer is stressed on its last syllable (re-FER), so the r is doubled.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Double the LAST consonant, not the f.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Keep the e of the -ed ending.

items.stem: Add -ing to offer. Which spelling is correct?

options.label: C
options.rationale: Keep the double f of the base word.

options.label: D

items.stem: Add -al to arrive. Which spelling is correct?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

items.stem: Add -able to manage. Which spelling is correct?

items.stem: Which shows the correct way to split fantastic into syllables?
